stem: A request enters an API container app, which calls an orchestrator, which calls Azure OpenAI. In distributed tracing terms, what links these three into a single view?

options.text: One trace id shared by all spans, with each span carrying the id of its parent span
One span id shared by all services, with each trace nested inside the previous trace
A correlation cookie issued by the first service and echoed by the others
Matching timestamps, which Azure Monitor uses to infer the call order

explanation: A trace is the whole journey; a span is one unit of work within it. Every span carries the same trace id and points at its parent, which is what lets Application Insights redraw the call tree rather than just listing events. Timestamps alone cannot do this — concurrent calls would be indistinguishable.

whyWrong.B: The nesting runs the other way: spans nest inside one trace.
whyWrong.C: Cookies are a browser mechanism and play no part in service-to-service correlation.
whyWrong.D: Ordering by time cannot tell you who called whom, and clock skew makes it worse.

stem: Two services are instrumented but their telemetry appears as separate, unrelated operations in Application Insights. Which HTTP header should be propagated to fix this?

options.text: `traceparent`, the W3C Trace Context header carrying the trace id, parent span id and flags
`x-ms-request-id`, which Azure services return on every response
`x-ms-client-request-id`, set by the calling SDK per operation
`Authorization`, whose token subject is used to group operations

explanation: W3C Trace Context is the standard OpenTelemetry and Azure Monitor both speak, and `traceparent` is the header that carries the context across a process boundary. If it is stripped — by a gateway, or by a hand-rolled `HttpClient` that builds a fresh request — the downstream span starts a brand new trace, which is exactly the symptom described.

whyWrong.B: `x-ms-request-id` identifies a single service-side request for support purposes; it does not chain calls.
whyWrong.C: `x-ms-client-request-id` is useful for correlating with a specific SDK call, but it is not the trace context.
whyWrong.D: Grouping by identity would merge unrelated requests from the same caller.

hint: Three of these identify one request. Only one describes a request's position in a larger call tree.

stem: Adaptive sampling is enabled on a high-volume service. A developer worries that request counts in dashboards will now be wrong. What actually happens?

options.text: Each retained item records an item count, and Application Insights scales aggregates back up, so counts stay approximately correct
Counts are reported as sampled and must be multiplied manually in every query
Sampling only drops trace-level logs, so request counts are unaffected
Counts are exact, because sampling is applied at query time rather than at ingestion

explanation: Sampling stores a representative subset and stamps each stored item with how many it stands for, so `summarize count()` and the built-in charts compensate automatically. What you lose is the individual dropped item — which matters when you go looking for one specific failed request, not when you are reading a rate.

whyWrong.B: The scaling is built in; manual multiplication would double-count.
whyWrong.C: Sampling applies to requests and dependencies as well, and it keeps related items together by operation id.
whyWrong.D: Adaptive sampling happens in the SDK before ingestion, which is precisely why the item count exists.

stem: Complete the KQL query that finds the slowest outbound calls to Azure OpenAI over the last hour, reported as a 95th percentile per target.
code:
[1]
| where timestamp > ago(1h)
| where target contains "openai"
| summarize [2](duration, 95) by target
| order by percentile_duration_95 desc

blanks.label: Blank 1 — the table holding outbound calls made by the app

explanation: `requests` is traffic coming in; `dependencies` is calls going out, which is where a slow model deployment shows up. `percentile(duration, 95)` is the right shape for a latency question — an average hides the tail, and a max is a single unlucky call.

stem: An ASP.NET Core service should send traces, metrics and logs to Application Insights using OpenTelemetry, with the least custom wiring. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Add the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro and call `builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry().UseAzureMonitor()`
Configure a raw OTLP exporter pointed at the Application Insights ingestion endpoint
Write a custom `ITelemetryProcessor` that forwards OpenTelemetry activities
Enable diagnostic settings on the app and let the platform export application traces

explanation: The distro is the supported one-liner: it wires the exporter, the standard instrumentation libraries and the sampler in a single call, and it is what Microsoft points you at for new applications. Anything more manual is extra surface to maintain for the same result.

whyWrong.B: Pointing OTLP directly at the ingestion endpoint is not the supported path and skips the correlation the distro sets up.
whyWrong.C: `ITelemetryProcessor` belongs to the classic Application Insights SDK, not to OpenTelemetry.
whyWrong.D: Diagnostic settings export platform logs and metrics; they do not capture in-process application traces.

stem: An app reads its settings from Azure App Configuration, where one entry is a Key Vault reference to a database password. The app's managed identity has App Configuration Data Reader. Reads of that one entry fail. Why?

options.text: A Key Vault reference stores only the secret's URI — the app resolves it itself, so its identity also needs permission on the key vault
Key Vault references require the App Configuration store's own identity, which cannot be granted to the app
App Configuration Data Reader excludes Key Vault references; App Configuration Data Owner is required
Key Vault references are only resolvable from App Service and Functions, not from containers

explanation: App Configuration never holds the secret value. The reference is a pointer, and the client library dereferences it using the application's identity — so the app needs both App Configuration Data Reader and a Key Vault secrets read permission. Two grants, one lookup.

whyWrong.B: The resolution happens client-side with the app's identity, not the store's.
whyWrong.C: Escalating the App Configuration role changes nothing, because the failure is on the key vault side.
whyWrong.D: Any client using the App Configuration provider can resolve references, containers included.

docs.title: Use Key Vault references in App Configuration

hint: Follow the secret value itself. Ask which service ever actually holds it.

stem: A compliance requirement states that no one — including a subscription owner — may permanently remove a secret before its retention period has elapsed. Which key vault setting delivers this?

options.text: Purge protection, which blocks purging a soft-deleted secret until the retention period expires
Soft delete, which is what keeps deleted secrets recoverable
A resource lock of type CanNotDelete on the key vault
Removing the Purge permission from every access policy and role assignment

explanation: Soft delete makes a deleted secret recoverable, but a sufficiently privileged principal can still purge it. Purge protection removes that escape hatch for the retention window — and note that once enabled it cannot be turned off, which is the point and also the thing to be sure about before enabling it.

whyWrong.B: Soft delete alone leaves purge available, which is exactly what the requirement forbids.
whyWrong.C: A lock protects the vault resource, not individual soft-deleted secrets, and an owner can remove the lock.
whyWrong.D: Permissions can be re-granted by an owner, so this is a policy, not a guarantee.

stem: Six container apps across three resource groups must all read the same set of secrets, and the role assignments should be made once rather than six times. Which identity approach fits?

options.text: A user-assigned managed identity shared by all six apps, granted the role once
A system-assigned managed identity on each app, with a role assignment per app
One app registration with a client secret, shared across the six apps
A system-assigned identity on one app, with the other five using its client id

explanation: A user-assigned identity is a standalone resource: create it, grant it access once, then attach it to as many apps as you like. A system-assigned identity is created and destroyed with its resource and cannot be shared, which is what makes it the wrong tool for a fleet.

whyWrong.B: Correct but not what was asked — this is six identities and six role assignments to keep in step.
whyWrong.C: A client secret is exactly the credential managed identities exist to remove.
whyWrong.D: A system-assigned identity cannot be borrowed by another resource; only the resource it belongs to can obtain its tokens.

stem: A user reports a failed request and gives you the time and the operation id. Put the investigation steps into the most efficient order.

options.text: Find the request in `requests` by `operation_Id`
List every telemetry item sharing that `operation_Id` to rebuild the call tree
Inspect the failing `dependencies` row for the downstream call that errored
Read the `exceptions` row linked to that dependency for the stack trace

explanation: Start from the known identifier rather than from a time window: locate the request, expand it into the full operation, narrow to the dependency that actually failed, then read the exception. Working the other way — scanning exceptions first — buries you in unrelated failures from the same period.
